objectives.label: Equality of ordered pairs
objectives.description: Find unknown values by using equality of ordered pairs, equating first projections and second projections.

objectives.label: Cartesian product of finite sets
objectives.description: Find the cartesian product X×Y and X² of finite sets, determine the number of its elements, and compare X×Y with Y×X.

objectives.label: Arrow and cartesian diagrams
objectives.description: Represent a cartesian product of finite sets by an arrow diagram and a cartesian diagram.

objectives.label: Graphing products of infinite sets
objectives.description: Represent N×N, Z×Z, Q×Q and R×R on a perpendicular graphical net, identify points as ordered pairs, and locate them by quadrant or axis.

entries.text: You have previously studied relation between two variables x, y

A.why: Assumed prior knowledge introducing the lesson.

B.why: Assumed earlier knowledge of relations between x and y.

entries.text: In each ordered pair $(a, b)$, a is called the first projection, and b is called the second projection.

A.why: Defines first and second projections, which are equated to solve ordered-pair equality.

B.why: Defines first and second projections used to equate pairs.

entries.text: Each ordered pair is represented by one and only one point in the coordinate plane.

A.why: Each ordered pair is one point in the coordinate plane, as in graphing.

B.why: Each ordered pair is one point, as in the graphing activities filed under objective 1.

entries.text:
If $a 
eq b$ then $(a, b) 
eq (b, a)$. (The page asks 'Why?', no answer printed.) $a 
eq b \Rightarrow (a,b) 
eq (b,a)$

A.why: Ordered pairs with a≠b are unequal when swapped, a fact about ordered-pair equality.

B.why: Order matters, so (a,b) ≠ (b,a) when a ≠ b.

entries.text: The ordered pair $(a, b)$ is not equal to the set $\{a, b\}$. $(a,b) \neq \{a,b\}$

A.why: Distinguishes an ordered pair from a set, which belongs with ordered-pair equality.

B.why: Ordered pair differs from a set, groundwork for pair equality.

entries.text: Table of X×Y: rows are first projection (a, b), columns are second projection (-1, 0, 3). ×, -1, 0, 3 / a, (a, -1), (a, 0), (a, 3) / b, (b, -1), (b, 0), (b, 3)

A.why: Table listing the elements of X×Y.

B.why: Lists X × Y for the worked example.

entries.text: Table of Y×X: rows are first projection (-1, 0, 3), columns are second projection (a, b). ×, a, b / -1, (-1, a), (-1, b) / 0, (0, a), (0, b) / 3, (3, a), (3,b)

A.why: Table listing the elements of Y×X for comparison with X×Y.

B.why: Lists Y × X for the worked example.

entries.text:
$X	imes Y
eq Y	imes X$ where $X
eq Y$. $X	imes Y
eq Y	imes X$

A.why: States that X×Y differs from Y×X when X≠Y.

B.why: Compares X×Y with Y×X.

entries.text: The number of elements of X×Y equals that of Y×X, which equals the product of the numbers of elements of X and Y. $n(X\times Y)=n(Y\times X)=n(X)\times n(Y)$

A.why: Gives the number of elements of X×Y as n(X)×n(Y).

B.why: Number of elements of X×Y and Y×X.

entries.text: n denotes the number of set elements.

A.why: Notation n for number of elements, used to count elements of products.

B.why: Notation n for counting elements of the product.

entries.text: If $(k,m)\in X\times Y$ then $k\in X$, $m\in Y$. $(k,m)\in X\times Y\Rightarrow k\in X,\ m\in Y$

A.why: Says what membership in X×Y means for the components of a pair.

B.why: Components of a pair in X × Y belong to X and Y.

entries.text: If X is a non-empty set, then $X\times X=\{(a,b):a,b\in X\}$. $X\times X=\{(a,b):a,b\in X\}$

A.why: Defines X×X for a finite set.

B.why: Defines X × X for a finite set.

entries.text: $X\times X$ is written $X^2$ and read 'X two'.

A.why: Notation X² for X×X.

B.why: Notation X² for X × X.

entries.text: Venn diagram: a black circle labelled Z contains 5, 6 and 2; a green oval labelled Y contains 2 and 3 and overlaps Z (2 in the overlap); a separate pink circle labelled X contains 1.

A.why: Venn diagram of sets X, Y, Z that is not about the product's representation.

B.why: Venn diagram of sets, prior knowledge not about the product.

entries.text: Arrow diagram for X × Y: left oval X containing 1 and 2, right oval Y containing 3, 4, 5. Arrows from 1 to 3, 4, 5 and from 2 to 3, 4, 5 (six arrows). Labelled X × Y below.

A.why: Arrow diagram of X×Y.

B.why: Arrow diagram for X × Y.

entries.text: Cartesian diagram (perpendicular graphical net) for X × Y: X = 1, 2 along the horizontal axis (bottom), Y = 3, 4, 5 along the vertical axis (left). Grid intersection points marked and labelled (1,3), (2,3), (1,4), (2,4), (1,5), (2,5). Labelled X × Y.

A.why: Cartesian diagram of X×Y.

B.why: Cartesian diagram for X × Y.

entries.text: Arrow Diagram for X × X: three points 3 (top), 4 (bottom right), 8 (bottom left); arrows between each pair of points in both directions, and a loop (buttonhole) at each of 3, 4 and 8.

A.why: Arrow diagram of X×X.

B.why: Arrow diagram for X × X.

entries.text: If n(X) = 3, then n(X × X) = 3 × 3 = 9. $n(X)=3 \Rightarrow n(X\times X)=3\times 3=9$

A.why: Counts the elements of X×X for n(X)=3.

B.why: Number of elements of X × X from n(X).

entries.text: Step 1: Draw two perpendicular straight lines, one horizontal (xx') and the other vertical (yy'), intersecting at point O.

A.why: Step to draw the perpendicular lines for the net.

B.why: Step for drawing the perpendicular axes of the net.

entries.text: Step 2: Represent the natural numbers N on each of the horizontal and vertical lines, starting with the origin O which represents zero.

A.why: Step to represent N on both axes.

B.why: Step for representing N on the axes of the net.

entries.text: Step 3: Draw vertical and horizontal lines from the points representing the natural numbers; the points of intersection form the perpendicular graphical net of the cartesian product N × N.

A.why: Step to form the net of N×N.

B.why: Step for building the N × N perpendicular net.

entries.text: Grid with axes x'x and y'y, origin O, numbers 1 to 5 marked on both axes. Point A at (3, 2), point B at (0, 4) on the y-axis, point C on the x-axis at about 5, and O at origin.

A.why: Grid of N×N with points read as ordered pairs.

B.why: N × N net with points A, B, C, O identified as ordered pairs.

entries.text: Each point of this net represents one of the ordered pairs in the cartesian product N × N.

A.why: Each net point is an ordered pair of N×N.

B.why: Each point of the net represents a pair of N × N.

entries.text: Represent the set of integers on each of the horizontal and vertical lines, where the point O represents the ordered pair (0, 0).

A.why: Represents Z on both axes for Z×Z.

B.why: Steps for representing Z on the axes of the Z × Z net.

entries.text: Each point of the net represents one of the pairs in the cartesian product Z × Z.

A.why: Each net point is a pair of Z×Z.

B.why: Each point of the net represents a pair of Z × Z.

entries.text: This net is known as the coordinate plane of Z × Z.

A.why: Names the net the coordinate plane of Z×Z.

B.why: Names the net as the coordinate plane of Z × Z.

entries.text: Coordinate plane of Z × Z with axes x'x and y'y, integers from -4 to 4 marked. Points: A at about (3, 3), B at about (3, -2), C at about (-3, 1), D at about (-3, -4).

A.why: Z×Z plane with points to identify as ordered pairs.

B.why: Z × Z coordinate plane with points as ordered pairs.

entries.text: The horizontal straight line xx' is called the x-axis.

A.why: Defines the x-axis of the graphical net.

B.why: Names the x-axis of the graphical net.

entries.text: The vertical straight line yy' is called the y-axis.

A.why: Defines the y-axis of the graphical net.

B.why: Names the y-axis of the graphical net.

entries.text: Perpendicular axes with x-axis (x, x') and y-axis (y, y') meeting at O, divided into four quadrants: first quadrant x > 0, y > 0 (top right); second quadrant x < 0, y > 0 (top left); third quadrant x < 0, y < 0 (bottom left); fourth quadrant x > 0, y < 0 (bottom right). Axes marked with numbers from -4 to 4.

A.why: Shows the four quadrants for locating points.

B.why: Four quadrants of the coordinate plane used to locate points.

entries.text: Square grid with x-axis and y-axis, origin O, axes marked -4 to 4. Points plotted: A (3, 3) top right, D (-4, 3) top left, C (-4, -2) bottom left, B (3, -2) bottom right, E (0, -3) on y-axis, F (2, 0) on x-axis.

A.why: Points located by quadrant or axis.

B.why: Points A–F plotted as ordered pairs in the plane, including on the axes.

objectives.label: Write a relation as ordered pairs
objectives.description: Write a relation R from X to Y as a set of ordered pairs, a subset of X × Y, by applying the rule given for a R b, and decide whether a given pair satisfies R.

objectives.label: Represent relations by diagrams
objectives.description: Represent a relation from X to Y by an arrow diagram and by a cartesian diagram.

objectives.label: Relation on a set
objectives.description: Write and represent a relation on a set X (from X to itself) as a subset of X × X.

entries.text: Picture of people holding up books with the words 'Reading for all'. Decorative.

A.why: Decorative picture introducing the lesson.

B.why: Decorative 'Reading for all' picture.

entries.text: Arrow diagram from X = {a, b, c, d, e} to Y = {Science, art, culture, history}. Arrows: a to Science, a to culture, b to history, c to culture (read from figure: c's arrow appears to go to culture), e to history; d has no arrow. Arrow endpoints read from picture; verify.

A.why: Arrow diagram of a relation from X to Y.

B.why: Introductory arrow diagram illustrating the idea of a relation, before representation is taught.

entries.text: Arrow diagram from X={-1,1,2} to Y={2,4,6,8}: arrows -1→2, 1→6, 2→8.

A.why: Arrow diagram of the relation from X to Y in the worked example.

B.why: Arrow diagram of the relation from X to Y showing -1→2, 1→6, 2→8.

entries.text: Graph diagram (printed 'Graph digram') with X axis marked -1, 1, 2 and Y axis marked 2, 4, 6, 8; points plotted at (-1,2), (1,6), (2,8).

A.why: Cartesian (graph) diagram of a relation from X to Y.

B.why: Graph (cartesian) diagram of the relation from X to Y with points (-1,2), (1,6), (2,8).

entries.text: A relation from X to Y, where X, Y are two non-empty sets, connects some or all of the elements of X with some or all of the elements of Y.

A.why: General definition of a relation introducing the lesson, not tied to one skill.

B.why: General definition introducing what a relation from X to Y is, before any particular objective.

entries.text: X × Y is the set of ordered pairs where the first projection in each ordered pair belongs to X and the second projection belongs to Y. $X\times Y$

A.why: Defines X × Y, the set of ordered pairs of which a relation is a subset.

B.why: X × Y as the set of ordered pairs is the set whose subsets are the relations written as ordered pairs.

entries.text: Arrow diagram of R on X: on a number line with points -2, -1, 0, 1, 2 curved arrows join -2↔2, -1↔1 and a loop at 0; beside it an oval Venn-style diagram of X with elements 0 (self-loop), -1 and 1 joined by double arrows, -2 and 2 joined by double arrows.

A.why: Arrow diagram of a relation on the set X.

B.why: Arrow diagram of R on X (from X to itself) with loop at 0 illustrates a relation on a set.

entries.text: Cartesian diagram with both axes marked -2, -1, 0, 1, 2; points plotted at (-2,2), (-1,1), (0,0), (1,-1), (2,-2).

A.why: Cartesian diagram of a relation on X, a subset of X × X.

B.why: Cartesian diagram of the relation on X with both axes -2 to 2 represents a relation on a set.

objectives.label: Identify functions from relations
objectives.description: Decide whether a relation from X to Y, given as ordered pairs, an arrow diagram or a cartesian diagram, is a function, by checking that each element of X is connected to only one element of Y, and justify the decision.

objectives.label: Write functions symbolically
objectives.description: Write a function symbolically using f : X → Y, f : x ↦ y and f(x) = y, and as a set of ordered pairs, and represent it by an arrow diagram and a cartesian diagram.

objectives.label: Find domain, codomain and range
objectives.description: Determine the domain, codomain and range of a function, recognising that the range is a subset of the codomain.

entries.text: Three arrow diagrams, labelled (1), (2), (3), each from set X = {2, 3, 5, 7} to set Y = {1, 4, 6, 8, 9}. Arrows are drawn between X and Y in each diagram; the individual arrows are too small to read reliably (diagram 3 appears to have several arrows ending at 6 and 9).

A.why: Arrow diagrams from X to Y are used to decide which relations are functions.

B.why: Arrow diagrams from X to Y that introduce deciding which relations are functions.

entries.text: The function is denoted by one of the symbols f or m or Q, etc. The function f from the set X to the set Y is written mathematically as f : X → Y and is read as "f is a fuction from X to Y". $f : X \rightarrow Y$

A.why: Gives the symbol f : X → Y for writing a function.

B.why: Gives the symbol f : X → Y for writing a function.

entries.text: If f is a function from X to itself, we say that f is a function on X.

A.why: Defines a function on X, part of the function notation.

B.why: Naming convention: a function from X to itself is a function on X, used in symbolic writing.

entries.text: Arrow diagram of f on X: 3 has a loop to itself; 4 and 5 joined by arrows both ways (4→5 and 5→4); 6 has an arrow to 5. Read from figure; verify arrow directions. Printed caption 'Arrow digaram'.

A.why: Arrow diagram representing the function f on X from the worked example.

B.why: Arrow diagram representing the function f on X of the worked example.

entries.text: Cartesian diagram with X on horizontal axis (3,4,5,6) and X on vertical axis (3,4,5,6); dots at (3,3), (4,5), (5,4), (6,5). Read from figure; verify.

A.why: Cartesian diagram representing the same function f on X.

B.why: Cartesian diagram representing the function f on X with f(3)=3, f(4)=5, f(5)=4, f(6)=5.

entries.text: Three arrow diagrams (1), (2), (3) on X = {1,2,3,4}, with arrows among points 1, 2, 3, 4. Arrows cannot be read reliably; verify against image.

A.why: Arrow diagrams on X={1,2,3,4} to decide which represent a function.

B.why: Arrow diagrams on X to decide which represent a function.

entries.text: Three cartesian diagrams (1), (2), (3), axes 1 to 5 on both. (1): dots at about (2,2), (3,3), (4,4), (4,5)... (2): dots in row 3 at x=1,2,3,4,5. (3): dots at about (1,1), (3,2), (4,4), (5,5). Points read from figure; verify.

A.why: Cartesian diagrams to decide which represent a function.

B.why: Cartesian diagrams to decide which represent a function by checking each x has one y.

entries.text: The set X is called the domain of the function f.

A.why: Defines the domain of a function.

B.why: Defines the domain of f.

entries.text: The set Y is called the codomain of the function f.

A.why: Defines the codomain of a function.

B.why: Defines the codomain of f.

A.why: Arrow diagram used to find domain, codomain and range.

B.why: Arrow diagram where the codomain {2,3,5,7} has an element not an image, illustrating domain, codomain and range.

entries.text: The range is a subset of the codomain of the function.

A.why: States the range is a subset of the codomain.

B.why: States that the range is a subset of the codomain.

entries.text: Arrow diagram from X to Y. X = {2, 3, 4}; Y = {2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8}. Arrows: 2→4, 3→6, 4→8.

A.why: Arrow diagram showing range {4,6,8} as a subset of codomain.

B.why: Arrow diagram with codomain larger than the set of images shows range as a subset of codomain.

objectives.label: Identify polynomial and degree
objectives.description: Identify which functions are polynomial functions and state the degree of a polynomial function.

objectives.label: Evaluate function values
objectives.description: Calculate the values of a polynomial function at given real numbers by substitution.

objectives.label: Graph linear and constant functions
objectives.description: Represent a linear function or constant function graphically using a table of ordered pairs.

objectives.label: Graph quadratic functions
objectives.description: Represent a quadratic function graphically on an interval and state its axis of symmetry, vertex and maximum or minimum value.

entries.text: The degree of the polynomial is the highest power of the variable in the function rule.

A.why: Degree is defined as the highest power of the variable, which is what objective 1 asks students to state.

B.why: States how to find the degree of a polynomial.

A.why: Table of ordered pairs for the linear function f(x)=2x-3 used to graph it.

B.why: Table of ordered pairs for f(x)=2x-3.

entries.text: Square-net graph with X and Y axes; straight line with arrows at both ends through points (0,-3), (1,-1) and (2,1), passing the x-axis between 1 and 2 (at 1.5). Marked points shown in blue. Read from the image; verify.

A.why: Straight-line graph of the linear function f(x)=2x-3.

B.why: Graph of linear function f(x)=2x-3 from its table.

entries.text: It is enough to find two ordered pairs belonging to the function; it is preferred to find a third ordered pair to check the graph.

A.why: Says to find two or three ordered pairs when graphing a linear function.

B.why: Two ordered pairs suffice to graph a linear function, a third to check.

entries.text: If f: R → R, f(x) = ax, where a ≠ 0, then it is represented graphically by a straight line passing through the origin (0, 0). $f(x)=ax,\ a\neq 0$

A.why: States that f(x)=ax graphs as a straight line through the origin, a linear function.

B.why: Graph of f(x)=ax is a straight line through the origin.

entries.text: Values of the constant function f(x) = 3 for x = -1, 1, 2 x, -1, 1, 2 / y = f(x), 3, 3, 3

A.why: Table of values of the constant function f(x)=3 used for graphing.

B.why: Table of ordered pairs for the constant function f(x)=3.

entries.text: Coordinate grid with axes x'x and y'y, x-axis marks -2, -1, 1, 2, y-axis mark 3. A horizontal line with arrows at both ends at y = 3, with points plotted at x = -1, 1, 2.

A.why: Horizontal-line graph of the constant function f(x)=3.

B.why: Graph of constant function f(x)=3 as a horizontal line.

entries.text: The function f: R → R where f(x) = ax² + bx + c, with a, b, c real numbers and a ≠ 0, is called a quadratic function and it is a function of second degree. $f(x)=ax^2+bx+c,\ a\neq 0$

A.why: Defines the quadratic function, which the graphing examples that follow are about.

B.why: Defines the quadratic function, introducing the quadratic graphing objective.

entries.text: Table of values of f(x)=x² for x from 3 down to -3 x, 3, 2, 1, 0, -1, -2, -3 / y = f(x), 9, 4, 1, 0, 1, 4, 9

A.why: Ordered pairs for graphing the quadratic f(x)=x².

B.why: Table of values of f(x)=x² for graphing the quadratic.

entries.text: Cartesian plane with x'x and y'y axes; blue parabola with vertex at origin (0,0) opening upwards, passing through plotted points (±1,1), (±2,4), (±3,9); y-axis marked 1 to 10, x-axis marked -4 to 4.

A.why: Parabola of f(x)=x² with vertex at the origin.

B.why: Graph of f(x)=x², an upward parabola with vertex at origin.

entries.text: The curve of the function f is symmetrical about the y-axis and the equation of the symmetrical axis is x = 0. $x=0$

A.why: Gives the axis of symmetry x=0 of the curve of x².

B.why: Axis of symmetry of f(x)=x² is x=0.

entries.text: The coordinate of the vertex of the curve is (0, 0), and the minimum value of the function = 0. $(0,0)$

A.why: Gives the vertex (0,0) and minimum value 0 for f(x)=x².

B.why: Vertex (0,0) and minimum value of f(x)=x².

entries.text: The curve is open upwards when the coefficient of x² is positive (a > 0), and in this case the function has a minimum value equal to f(-b/2a). $f\left(\frac{-b}{2a}\right)$

A.why: Says an upward-opening curve (a>0) has a minimum value f(-b/2a).

B.why: Upward-opening curve when a>0 gives a minimum value.

entries.text: The curve is open downward when the coefficient of x² is negative (a < 0), and in this case the function has a maximum value equal to f(-b/2a). $f\left(\frac{-b}{2a}\right)$

A.why: Says a downward-opening curve (a<0) has a maximum value f(-b/2a).

B.why: Downward-opening curve when a<0 gives a maximum value.

entries.text: The curve is symmetric about the vertical line through the vertex of the curve, whose equation is X = -b/2a; this line is called the axis of symmetry of the function. $x=\frac{-b}{2a}$

A.why: Gives the axis of symmetry x=-b/2a of a quadratic curve.

B.why: States the axis of symmetry x=-b/2a of a quadratic curve.

entries.text: Table of values of y = f(x) for x from 3 to -3 x, 3, 2, 1, 0, -1, -2, -3 / y = f(x), -9, -4, -1, 0, -1, -4, -9

A.why: Ordered pairs for graphing the quadratic f(x)=-x².

B.why: Table of values for the quadratic f(x)=-x² used to draw the curve.

entries.text: Graph on x'x and y'y axes (grid) showing a downward-opening parabola with vertex at the origin (0,0), symmetric about the y-axis, passing through plotted points (±1,-1), (±2,-4), (±3,-9). x-axis labelled -4 to 4, y-axis labelled 1 to 9 downward (negative).

A.why: Downward-opening parabola of f(x)=-x² with vertex at the origin.

B.why: Graph of f(x)=-x² showing downward parabola with vertex at origin.
